title: What changes when you learn something
objectives: Find the outcomes that are left after a piece of news
Recompute a chance by counting inside what is left
Recognise news that does not change a chance

screens.title: What changes when you learn something
screens.prose: A die is rolled out of sight, and someone tells you one fact about it. Some faces are now impossible. We will see what that does to a chance.
A friend rolls a fair die behind a book. You cannot see it, but they tell you the result is even.

state.caption: Six faces, all equally likely before the news

screens.question: Is a 6 now more likely than before, less likely, or just as likely?

options.why: You kept all six faces in play. The news makes 1, 3 and 5 impossible, so 6 has fewer rivals.
You treated the news as working against 6. But 6 is even, so it survives while three rivals drop out.

hints.text: Which faces can the die still be showing?
The odd faces are now impossible.
Before the news, 6 was one face of six. After it, 6 is one face of three. Compare the two.

feedback.correct: The news rules out three faces, and 6 is not one of them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about which faces the news rules out.

explain.text: You noticed that 6 survives the news while 1, 3 and 5 do not. Fewer faces are left to share the whole chance, so each survivor gets a bigger share. We will put a number on it next.

screens.prose: Tap the faces to mark the ones the news still allows. Tap a face again to clear it.
screens.question: Mark every face that is still possible.

hints.text: Which numbers from 1 to 6 are even?
Every second face is even, starting from 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Mark every even face, and only those.

byKey.odd: You marked the odd faces. Those are the ones the news rules out.
byKey.only-six: You marked only 6. The news allows every even face, not just the one we asked about.
byKey.r1c1: 1 is odd, so the news rules it out.
byKey.r1c3: 3 is odd, so the news rules it out.
byKey.r1c5: 5 is odd, so the news rules it out.

explain.text: You marked 2, 4 and 6, the faces that agree with the news. The other three can no longer happen. Those three marked faces are all that is left to count.

screens.prose: The faces you marked are the outcomes that are left. We write $P(6 \mid \text{even})$ for the chance of a 6 **given** the roll is even.
screens.question: What is $P(6 \mid \text{even})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of a 6 given even
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{1}{3}$, or a decimal that rounds to 0.33.

hints.text: How many faces are left, and how many of them are a 6?
Only the three marked faces count now.
One face of the three left is a 6. Each is equally likely, so the chance is 1 out of 3.

feedback.correct: One face out of the three left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count only the faces that are left.

byKey.before: That is the chance before the news, one face of six. Only three faces are left now.
byKey.half: You split the even faces into 6 and not 6. There are two faces that are not 6, so it is 1 out of 3.

explain.text: You counted one 6 among the three faces left. So $P(6 \mid \text{even}) = \tfrac{1}{3}$, up from $\tfrac{1}{6}$. The news doubled the chance by halving what is left.

screens.prose: A new roll. This time you hear the result is greater than 3. The diagram sorts the faces by both facts.
screens.question: What is the chance the roll is even, given it is greater than 3?

options.why: That is the chance before the news. Only 4, 5 and 6 are left, not all six faces.
You divided by all six faces. Only the three faces greater than 3 are left.
You counted the odd face left, 5. The question asks for the even ones, 4 and 6.

hints.text: Which faces are greater than 3?
The circle on the right holds every face greater than 3.
4, 5 and 6 are left. Two of them, 4 and 6, are even.

feedback.correct: Two of the three faces left, 4 and 6, are even.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only the faces greater than 3, then count the even ones.

explain.text: You kept the right-hand circle, faces 4, 5 and 6. The overlap holds the even ones, 4 and 6. So the chance is $\tfrac{2}{3}$, up from $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

screens.prose: Same news: the roll is greater than 3. Now ask about a face the news rules out.
screens.question: What is the chance the roll is a 1, given it is greater than 3?

widget.label: Chance of a 1 given greater than 3
widget.accept: 0 exactly. A 1 is not greater than 3.

hints.text: Is 1 one of the faces that are left?
1 sits outside both circles.
None of the three faces left is a 1. Zero faces out of three gives a chance of 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for 1 among the faces that are left.

byKey.before: That is the chance before the news. A 1 is not greater than 3, so it is gone.
byKey.third: You gave 1 a share of the three faces left. But 1 is not one of them.

explain.text: You looked for 1 among 4, 5 and 6 and found nothing. News can push a chance all the way to zero. That is the edge case: an outcome the news rules out has chance 0.

screens.prose: A new roll, new news: the result is at most 4. Before the news, the chance of an even roll was $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
screens.question: Given the roll is at most 4, what happens to the chance it is even?

options.why: You expected any news to change the chance. Two of the four faces left are even: the same share as before.
You counted the even face that dropped out, 6. But an odd face, 5, dropped out too.

hints.text: Which faces are at most 4, and which of those are even?
The right-hand circle holds 1, 2, 3 and 4.
Four faces are left. Two of them, 2 and 4, are even. Compare $\tfrac{2}{4}$ with $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

feedback.correct: Two of the four faces left are even, the same share as before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the even faces among the four that are left.

byKey.rises: You assumed news always changes a chance. Here two of the four faces left are even, exactly half.

explain.text: You counted 2 and 4 among the four faces left: $\tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2}$. The faces removed, 5 and 6, were half even, like the whole die, so the chance held. News changes a chance only when the outcomes it removes hold a different share of the event than before.

screens.prose: Every time, you did the same two things. Keep the outcomes the news allows, then count inside them. With equally likely outcomes: $$P(A \mid B) = \frac{\text{outcomes in both } A \text{ and } B}{\text{outcomes in } B}$$
screens.question: In this rule, what goes on the bottom of the fraction?

options.text: The outcomes in the event you are asking about
options.why: You put $A$ on the bottom. The news, $B$, decides what is left to count in.

options.text: Every outcome, as before the news
options.why: You kept the whole sample space. The news rules some outcomes out, so they leave the bottom too.

hints.text: On the die screens, what did you divide by?
You divided by the faces that were left after the news: 3 even faces, or 3 faces above 3.

feedback.correct: The news sets the new whole.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what you divided by on the earlier screens.

explain.text: You divided by 3 for the even faces and by 4 for the faces at most 4. Each time, the bottom was what the news allowed. The top was the part of that which also matched the question.

screens.prose: A dataset covers 200 trading days of one stock. Each day was high or normal volume, and up or not up. The diagram gives the counts.
screens.question: You pick a high-volume day at random. What is the chance it was an up day?

widget.label: Chance of an up day given high volume

hints.text: How many days were high volume?
The left circle holds every high-volume day: 24 plus 56.
There were 80 high-volume days, and 56 of them were up. Divide 56 by 80.

feedback.correct: 56 of the 80 high-volume days were up days.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only the high-volume days, then count the up days among them.

byKey.all-up: That is the share of all 200 days that were up. The news keeps only the high-volume days.
byKey.wrong-bottom: You divided by the 120 up days. The condition is high volume, so divide by the 80 high-volume days.
byKey.all-days: You divided by all 200 days. Only the 80 high-volume days are left.

explain.text: You kept the 80 high-volume days and found 56 up days among them: $\tfrac{56}{80} = 0.7$. Across all days the share was $\tfrac{120}{200} = 0.6$. So high volume tells you something about the direction in this dataset.

ideas: News rules some outcomes out. What is left is the only thing we count in.
A chance given news is a count inside what is left, over the size of what is left.
News can raise a chance, lower it to zero, or leave it alone.

formula.name: Chance given news
formula.tex: P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{\text{outcomes in } A \text{ and } B}{\text{outcomes in } B}
formula.note: For equally likely outcomes. Read $P(A \mid B)$ as the chance of $A$ given $B$.

summary.trap: News does not always change a chance. Check the share inside what is left before you decide.

quiz.prose: One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. You learn it is red.
quiz.question: What is the chance it is a heart?

options.why: That is the chance before the news. Only the 26 red cards are left.
You treated red as meaning hearts. Diamonds are red too.
You counted one heart. There are 13 hearts among the 26 red cards.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the hearts among the red cards.

explain.text: Learning the card is red leaves 26 cards: 13 hearts and 13 diamonds. So the chance of a heart is $\tfrac{13}{26} = \tfrac{1}{2}$, up from $\tfrac{1}{4}$.

quiz.prose: A fair die is rolled. You learn the result is at least 3.
quiz.question: What is the chance it is a 6? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of a 6 given at least 3

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the faces that are at least 3.

byKey.before: That is the chance before the news. Only 3, 4, 5 and 6 are left.
byKey.boundary: You left out 3. At least 3 includes 3 itself, so four faces are left.

explain.text: At least 3 keeps 3, 4, 5 and 6: four faces. One of them is a 6. So the chance is $\tfrac{1}{4}$.

quiz.prose: A fair die is rolled. You learn the result is odd.
quiz.question: Before the news, a roll of at most 3 had chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$. What is it now?

options.why: You assumed the news cannot matter. Two of the three odd faces, 1 and 3, are at most 3.
You counted the odd face above 3, which is 5. The question asks for faces at most 3.
You divided by all six faces. Only the three odd faces are left.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the odd faces, then count those at most 3.

explain.text: Odd leaves 1, 3 and 5. Two of them, 1 and 3, are at most 3. So the chance rises from $\tfrac{1}{2}$ to $\tfrac{2}{3}$.
